strengths: The paper targets an important, underexplored problem: maintaining instruction-conditioned expressive style across multi-turn role-play TTS, beyond intelligibility and speaker similarity.

MCLP is an intuitive and potentially useful idea: repurposing a pretrained audio language model's continuation likelihood as a dense reference-based signal for style evaluation and reinforcement learning.

The proposed pipeline is coherent. It combines supervised fine-tuning, GRPO, a style reward, and an intelligibility constraint; the reward ablations clearly expose style-only reward hacking and the opposing tendency of content-only optimization.

The reported dataset is substantial (1,435 hours and approximately 311,000 scenes), uses video-level train/test separation, and includes scene, character, and multi-turn annotations. If released with appropriate permissions and documentation, it could be a useful resource.

The main results are quantitatively strong: the proposed system improves CER, Pinyin WER, MCLP, and subjective MOS over the evaluated baselines. The paper is generally well organized, and its figures and tables are readable.
weaknesses: The central claim that MCLP measures style is not adequately established. Conditioning ground-truth audio on candidate audio can reflect speaker identity, timbre, recording channel, duration, acoustic quality, tokenization artifacts, and phonetic realization—not only style. Holding the transcript fixed does not eliminate these factors, and no controlled perturbation study disentangles them.

The information-theoretic justification is technically flawed. Expected log likelihood equals negative conditional entropy minus KL divergence, whereas Equation 3 displays a positive KL term. More fundamentally, model cross-entropy is not mutual information without a well-specified joint distribution and calibrated density model; the assertion that remaining mutual information is dominated by style is unsupported.

Evaluation is partly circular because MCLP is both the RL optimization target and a principal reported metric. The independent human study is too limited to resolve this: it covers only about 30 scenarios, lacks rater agreement and full protocol details, and does not report standard rank correlations or matched-prompt analyses. Forming all pairwise comparisons also creates statistically dependent observations, yet bin counts and the confidence-interval procedure are omitted.

The subjective comparison does not cleanly isolate style. Systems differ substantially in intelligibility, and listeners cannot reliably ignore unintelligible content even when instructed to disregard audio quality. Some baseline outputs are additionally resynthesized through the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer with ground-truth audio prompts, while the proposed system is not marked as undergoing the same procedure, leaving the fairness and effect of this transformation unclear. There is also no subjective SFT-versus-RL ablation.

Generalization evidence is weak. The split is by video rather than drama series or character, so episodes, characters, actors, and production conditions may occur in both training and test data. Character profiles are inferred from complete episode scripts, potentially including the evaluated utterances. The paper provides no evaluation on unseen series, external data, controlled style mismatches, or alternative MCLP evaluator models.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The 300-million-hour LALM used to compute MCLP is not identified or documented sufficiently, and possible overlap between its pretraining data and WenetSpeech is not addressed. RL duration, update count, batch configuration, clipping parameter, decoding limits, checkpoint selection, seeds, and variance across runs are absent. The internal neutral-style classifier is also undocumented, and the dataset and code are only promised for future release.

There are material inconsistencies in the reward description: the equations define a CER penalty, while the tables and discussion call it a WER reward. Hyperparameter sensitivity for the large bias, penalty weight, and hard CER threshold is not studied. The ablations also do not compare against simpler independent style rewards or likelihood baselines, making it difficult to attribute gains specifically to the proposed formulation.

Dataset annotation quality is insufficiently validated. Scene and character labels are generated automatically after diarization and source separation, but no human audit, annotation-accuracy estimate, failure analysis, or filtering statistics for these stages are reported. Calling the resulting corpus high quality is therefore premature.

The ethics and limitations treatment is unacceptable for this application. The work uses and proposes releasing large amounts of YouTube drama speech, yet does not discuss copyright, licenses, performer consent, privacy, redistribution rights, voice impersonation, or misuse for convincing character/actor cloning. The generic impact statement claiming that no consequences require highlighting fails to engage with obvious risks.

MCLP is an interesting and potentially useful idea: using conditional audio-token likelihood as a reference-based signal could provide a denser reward than categorical emotion classifiers.

The reward-component ablations expose meaningful behavior: MCLP-only optimization produces severe content failure, while content-only optimization reduces the reported style score. This supports the practical need for a hybrid objective.
The proposed dataset is large (1,435 hours and roughly 311,000 scenes), and the paper reports human judgments in addition to automatic metrics.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central interpretation of MCLP as a style metric is not established. Conditional likelihood can reflect speaker identity, timbre, codec artifacts, duration, recording conditions, or general predictability. Holding the transcript fixed does not make variation in mutual information 'dominated by style.' The paper lacks controlled perturbations that independently vary style, speaker, content, and audio quality, as well as comparisons with established prosody or audio-embedding metrics.

The information-theoretic derivation contains a substantive error: under the data distribution, E[log P_theta] equals negative conditional entropy minus KL divergence, not negative entropy plus KL as written in Eq. 3. More fundamentally, mutual information between two utterances is not shown to identify stylistic consistency, and the density-estimation assumption is neither tested nor sufficient for that conclusion.

The main automatic evidence is circular: the model is optimized using MCLP and then its style improvement is primarily demonstrated using the same MCLP evaluator. The reported gain is therefore expected even if the reward is imperfect. Independent human evaluation of the SFT-versus-RL comparison, or evaluation with unrelated style metrics, is missing.

The human validation is too small and underspecified for the central claims. It uses only 31 samples, and the meaning of '30 valid responses' is unclear relative to 32 annotators. The paper omits assignment design, rating counts per system, randomization and blinding details, inter-rater reliability, and significance tests between systems. Figure 5 constructs many dependent pairwise comparisons from the same ratings, but gives neither bin counts nor a confidence-interval procedure accounting for this dependence; a standard sample-level rank correlation would be more defensible.

Experimental comparisons are heavily confounded. The proposed system is trained specifically on the new corpus, whereas the baselines are general-purpose systems with no comparable adaptation. There is no matched SFT baseline from another architecture, no test across alternative MCLP backbones, and no evidence that gains generalize beyond Mandarin television drama. Claims of 'significant' improvement are made without statistical tests.

Dataset validity is insufficiently assessed. Scene boundaries are derived from silence gaps, character profiles are inferred automatically from transcripts, and scene descriptions are generated by a vision-language model, yet no human audit or annotation-accuracy measurements are reported. A video-level split can still place episodes or characters from the same series in both training and test sets, and possible overlap between the 300-million-hour evaluator pretraining corpus and the test dramas is not investigated.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper says the dataset 'will be open source' but provides no artifact. It omits crucial details about the MCLP model and its 300-million-hour training data, the internal style classifier, RL duration and update schedule, decoding settings, random seeds, and prompts/settings for several baselines. GPT-Audio is not identified by a reproducible model version. Terminology also alternates between CER and WER for the content reward.

The claimed significance is promising but presently limited because MCLP requires a ground-truth audio reference for the same transcript and relies on an enormous proprietary evaluator. The paper does not establish robustness across references, evaluator sizes, speakers, domains, or languages.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims overreach the evidence: MCLP is called 'interpretable' and 'explainable' without analysis of what acoustic factors drive it; 'approaching the naturalness of ground truth' is asserted although annotators were instructed to ignore naturalness-related audio quality; and reward/content terminology is inconsistent.

Research ethics are materially under-addressed. The dataset is derived from YouTube dramas and includes actors' voices, inferred identities, and character profiles, yet the manuscript discusses neither licenses and redistribution rights nor consent, privacy, performer rights, impersonation/deepfake risks, or safeguards. The generic impact statement claiming that no consequence needs highlighting is inadequate for expressive voice generation and the proposed release of scraped dramatic speech. These unresolved issues further preclude acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality: MCLP is a clever use of a pretrained audio language model’s continuation likelihood as both an evaluation metric and a dense reinforcement-learning reward for expressive role-play TTS.

Significance: The paper targets an important and underdeveloped problem—maintaining context-dependent speaking style across multi-turn dialogue—and constructs a substantial corpus of approximately 1,435 hours, 311k scenes, and 2.28M utterances.

Soundness: The hybrid style/content reward is well motivated. Table 3 usefully exposes concrete reward-hacking behavior: style-only optimization raises MCLP but drives CER above 59%, while content-only optimization improves intelligibility but reduces MCLP.

Evaluation: The proposed system substantially improves CER, Pinyin WER, MCLP, and subjective MOS over the reported baselines. Evaluation with professional native-Chinese listeners is a positive feature.
Presentation: The manuscript is polished and easy to follow, with clear diagrams, formal definitions, dataset statistics, training details, ablations, and data-construction prompts.
weaknesses: Soundness: The information-theoretic justification contains a sign error. Under the data distribution, E[log P_theta] equals negative conditional entropy minus KL divergence, not negative entropy plus KL as written in Eq. 3. More fundamentally, conditioning likelihood does not establish that variation is dominated by style: MCLP can reflect speaker identity, timbre, recording conditions, codec compatibility, prosody, or evaluator-model bias even when transcripts match.

The central empirical validation of MCLP is insufficient. Figure 5 uses all pairwise comparisons from a small 31-sample subjective set, but does not report a standard utterance-level correlation, comparisons with alternative style/prosody metrics, statistical methodology for the confidence intervals, or treatment of the strong dependence among pairwise observations.

Evidence for the RL contribution is partly circular: the model is optimized using MCLP and then judged using MCLP. The paper reports no human MOS ablation comparing SFT, content-only RL, style-only RL, and the full reward. Thus the experiments show that the complete system sounds better than generic baselines, but do not convincingly establish that MCLP reward causes a perceptual style improvement.

Baseline fairness and generality are limited. The proposed system receives 1,435 hours of task-specific SFT plus RL, whereas the principal baselines are generic instruction-tuned systems. Results are reported for only one trainable backbone, and objective improvements lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis.

Dataset reliability is under-validated. Scene boundaries are inferred from silence and a 30-second cap, while character identities, profiles, and scene descriptions are automatically generated from diarization and foundation models. No human audit or accuracy measurements are reported. The discrepancy between 13,510 retrieved videos in the text and 8,556 video-available items in Table 1 is also unexplained.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: the exact MCLP evaluator, composition of its claimed 300-million-hour pretraining data, evaluator training configuration, internal neutral-style classifier, GPT-Audio version and prompting, random seeds, decoding details, and model checkpoints are not specified. Data and code are only promised for future release. The manuscript also inconsistently describes the content reward as CER versus WER.

Ethics and limitations are not appropriately treated. The dataset derives from real YouTube dramas and identifiable performers, yet the paper does not discuss copyright and licensing, performer consent, release rights, voice or character impersonation, misuse safeguards, privacy, or demographic bias. The generic impact statement that no consequences require highlighting is especially inadequate for a role-play voice-generation system. Overall, the idea is promising and the complete-system results are encouraging, but the unsupported specificity of MCLP as a style metric, circular evaluation, reproducibility gaps, and unresolved data ethics currently outweigh the paper’s merits.

strengths: Originality: MCLP is an interesting use of audio-language-model continuation likelihood as both a reference-based style metric and an RL reward. Applying it to multi-turn role-play TTS is a reasonably novel formulation.

Significance: Objective assessment of open-ended speaking style is an important problem, and the proposed 1,435-hour, 311k-scene corpus could be valuable if its data, annotations, and legal status are documented and released appropriately.

Soundness: The experiments include strong recent baselines, evaluations with and without audio history, a 900-scene test set, human ratings, and useful reward-component ablations. The ablations clearly expose MCLP-only reward hacking and show why the CER constraint is necessary.
The reported gains are large: the full method improves MOS from 3.178 after SFT to 3.576 after RL while reducing CER, and it outperforms the listed baselines on all reported automatic measures.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, the method and data pipeline are easy to follow, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges language/domain restrictions and noisy automatically generated annotations.
The impact statement recognizes impersonation and deceptive-audio risks and suggests watermarking and monitoring.
weaknesses: Soundness: Validation of the central metric is inadequate. Section 6.2 omits the number and provenance of utterances, systems represented, rating protocol, raw correlation coefficients, ties, and statistical model. Computing all possible utterance pairs creates strongly dependent observations, yet the paper reports ordinary binned confidence intervals without explaining how dependence was handled. A monotonic binned win-rate plot alone does not establish metric validity.

MCLP is not shown to isolate style. It can reflect speaker identity, recording quality, tokenizer reconstruction error, prosody, or the intrinsic predictability of the particular ground-truth token sequence. Calling the construction conceptually symmetric does not make its asymmetric conditional likelihood symmetric. Essential controls—same speaker/different style, different speaker/same style, degraded audio, transcript mismatch, reference reversal, and comparisons with established perceptual metrics—are absent.

The continuation model is trained on three million hours of unspecified speech. The sources, licenses, composition, filtering, optimization details, checkpoint, and possible overlap with the RP-TTS test material are not reported. Consequently, neither the metric nor the claimed held-out evaluation is presently auditable or reproducible.

Evaluation partially uses the optimized reward itself: the proposed system is trained against MCLP and then declared best using MCLP. The human study mitigates this circularity but is only 30 cases. The manuscript does not report per-condition MOS, listener/case assignment, inter-rater reliability, paired significance tests, or a hierarchical analysis accounting for repeated ratings. Confidence intervals may therefore substantially overstate precision.

Reward optimization has access to the ground-truth audio for each training query, so the observed gains could arise from matching reference-specific speaker/prosodic or acoustic cues rather than learning general adherence to textual role-play instructions. No held-out-instruction, unseen-series/character, or cross-dataset human evaluation disentangles these possibilities.

Baseline comparability is uncertain. Several systems are resynthesized through the Step-Audio tokenizer while others are not; prompt rewriting is undocumented; GPT-Audio lacks an exact model/version and decoding settings; and no naturalness or artifact rating is reported. Asking raters to disregard audio-quality differences cannot ensure that resynthesis and reward-hacking artifacts do not affect style judgments.

The split is only video-level. Related clips from the same series, episode, character, or actor may occur across training and test, which is especially problematic for character/style assessment. The paper already infers series and episode metadata but does not use it to construct a stricter split. Moreover, 72.8% of training scenes contain one speaker while the test set excludes them, and annotation accuracy is not quantified.

Reproducibility is poor for a 7B-model, 32-H800 study: random seeds, sampling/decoding details for evaluation, exact checkpoints, training duration, annotation instructions in Chinese, filtering-model details, and audio examples are missing. The abstract says the code is publicly available but provides no URL, and the dataset footnote likewise contains no accessible release information.

Ethics and data governance are underdeveloped. The dataset derives expressive voices and character identities from YouTube dramas, but the paper does not discuss copyright and licensing compatibility, performer consent, privacy/biometric voice concerns, redistribution conditions, takedown procedures, or whether generated character descriptions contain sensitive inferences. The generic misuse paragraph does not resolve these dataset-specific issues.

Presentation is polished overall, but several conclusions exceed the evidence: Appendix B only distinguishes self-prompted from previous-utterance prompting and does not establish broad cross-lingual style validity, while category/turn/speaker analyses report only the same optimized MCLP metric rather than independent human evidence. These issues affect the paper's central claim, so the weaknesses outweigh its promising idea and empirical scale.

strengths: The paper targets an important and relatively underexplored problem: maintaining expressive, context-appropriate speech across multi-turn role-play dialogue.
MCLP is a simple and potentially useful reference-based idea, and using the same signal for evaluation and reinforcement learning is an interesting contribution.
The dataset is large, and the manuscript clearly describes its construction pipeline, split strategy, annotation prompts, and basic statistics.

The experiments include diverse LALM and instruction-TTS baselines. The reward ablations are informative: optimizing MCLP alone causes severe content reward hacking, while the combined CER–MCLP reward substantially improves intelligibility and human ratings over SFT.
The paper is generally well organized and readable. It also candidly acknowledges its Mandarin/domain limitations, automatic-annotation noise, and possible misuse of expressive speech generation.
weaknesses: The central claim that MCLP measures style is not adequately established. Predicting ground-truth audio tokens from candidate audio can reflect speaker identity, timbre, recording conditions, tokenization artifacts, naturalness, or general acoustic similarity. Calling the tokenizer semantic and holding the transcript fixed does not isolate style, and the paper provides no controlled factor-disentanglement experiments.

The human validation of MCLP is underspecified and statistically questionable. The number and provenance of evaluated utterances, rating assignment, agreement, tie handling, and confidence-interval calculation are absent. Constructing all possible utterance pairs creates strongly dependent observations, yet Figure 5 appears to treat binned pairs as independent. Standard rank correlations, uncertainty over independent utterances, and comparisons against CAM++/Emo2Vec or other metrics are missing.

The validation does not test important counterexamples: same style with different speakers or channels, same speaker with deliberately changed style, degraded audio with preserved style, or lexical and prosodic perturbations. Consequently, the evidence cannot distinguish stylistic sensitivity from nuisance similarity.

The cross-lingual experiment is weak evidence: self-prompted synthesis reuses the target audio itself, whereas the comparison uses a different preceding utterance. The exact-match advantage is expected under many acoustic-similarity metrics and does not demonstrate that MCLP captures English style.

The main evaluation is partly circular because the proposed model is optimized with MCLP and then prominently evaluated by MCLP. The human study mitigates this only partially: it covers merely 30 cases, reports a single aggregated MOS despite two evaluation settings, gives no significance tests or case-level analysis, and likely produces overly narrow confidence intervals if individual ratings are treated as independent.

Baseline comparability is unclear. Several systems are resynthesized through the Step-Audio-2 tokenizer with ground-truth prompts, while others are not, and instruction-TTS systems receive rewritten prompts and are evaluated only without audio history. These unequal inference pipelines can affect timbre, artifacts, content, and perceived style.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the core contribution. The MCLP evaluator is additionally trained on three million hours of speech, but the corpus composition, licensing, optimization settings, filtering, and availability of its checkpoint are not specified. The internal style classifier used for RL-data selection is also undocumented, and several reward/GRPO implementation details are missing.

The automatically constructed dataset may be valuable, but annotation quality is not quantitatively audited. Silence-based scene boundaries, diarization, LLM-inferred character profiles, and video-derived scene descriptions can all fail systematically; notably, 72.8% of training scenes contain only one speaker, limiting the claimed multi-party nature.

The ethics discussion is too generic given the use of retrieved YouTube drama performances and actor voices. The paper does not address copyright and dataset licensing, performer consent, identity exposure, redistribution conditions, or concrete release safeguards. These omissions are material for a dataset and model intended to reproduce character-consistent expressive speech.

Overall, the idea and empirical gains are promising, but the unsupported construct validity of the proposed metric—together with weak statistical reporting, reproducibility gaps, and unresolved data ethics—undermines the paper's principal claims and prevents acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Original and practically useful formulation: MCLP turns a pretrained audio language model's continuation likelihood into both a reference-based style-consistency metric and a dense reinforcement-learning reward for role-play TTS.

The empirical results are promising. The proposed model substantially improves stylistic-fidelity MOS over the strongest reported multi-turn baseline (3.576 versus 2.484) and the strongest instruction-TTS baseline (3.576 versus 2.864), while also obtaining markedly lower CER.

The ablations are informative: SFT improves MOS from 1.856 to 3.178, the full RL method further raises it to 3.576, MCLP-only optimization causes severe reward hacking and over 59% CER, and CER-only optimization produces intelligible but perceptually flatter speech. This convincingly motivates the hybrid reward.

The work has meaningful scale and potential significance: the constructed corpus contains about 1,435 hours and 311,938 multi-turn scenes, while evaluation includes several recent LALM and instruction-TTS baselines, objective metrics, 48 valid professional-listener responses, and analyses by dialogue length, scene category, and speaker count.

The manuscript is clearly organized and visually polished, explains the training and reward pipeline well, reports important optimization hyperparameters, and includes an appropriate limitations section acknowledging language, domain, and automatic-annotation limitations.
weaknesses: The central validation of MCLP is under-specified and statistically weak. Section 6.2 does not state how many utterances or systems produced the samples, reports no standard rank or linear correlation, and constructs all possible pairs from shared utterances, which are not independent. Binned pairwise win rates can therefore produce misleadingly narrow confidence intervals. Correlations should be reported with utterance/session-level bootstrap intervals and compared against established proxy metrics.

MCLP has not been sufficiently disentangled from nuisance factors. Despite using a semantic tokenizer and a fixed transcript, the score may still respond to speaker identity, recording quality, duration, token predictability, or similarity to the continuation model's training distribution. Controlled tests that independently vary timbre, emotion, prosody, quality, and content—and a comparison against simpler likelihood or embedding baselines—are needed to substantiate the interpretation as stylistic consistency.

The subjective protocol leaves consequential ambiguities. Table 2 reports only one MOS column although objective results are separated into with- and without-history conditions; it is unclear how the 10 no-history and 20 history cases are aggregated and how methods evaluated on different subsets remain directly comparable. Rater/sample assignment, per-utterance rating counts, randomization, inter-rater reliability, and paired significance tests are also absent. Only 30 cases are used despite a 900-scene test set.

Evaluation on the same MCLP model used as the optimization reward is inherently circular. Human MOS mitigates this concern, but independent perceptual evaluation is small, and the large MCLP gains—especially the fine-grained appendix analyses—cannot independently validate generalization. Evaluation with a separately trained metric or held-out human preference benchmark would strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a central component: the continuation model is further trained on three million hours, but the manuscript does not describe the data composition, splits, training hyperparameters, compute, or checkpoint availability. The RP-TTS pipeline also relies on an unspecified internal neutral-style classifier and automatically inferred character annotations. These omissions make exact reconstruction of MCLP and the training set difficult even though the downstream SFT/RL hyperparameters are reported.

The dataset raises ethical and governance questions not addressed by the impact statement. It is derived from YouTube drama performances and uses recognizable actors' voices and inferred character identities; the paper should clarify licenses, redistribution rights, performer consent, privacy handling, and whether release enables voice impersonation. The current discussion focuses mainly on downstream deceptive use and does not cover these data-origin risks.

Overall, this is a useful and promising contribution, but the limited validation of the proposed metric, ambiguous subjective comparison, and substantial reproducibility and data-governance gaps prevent a confident full accept.
